Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

author: Clankerusecase

            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Machine-cadence inbound scanning of FortiGate management/SSL-VPN endpoints AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects the article's MCP-driven discovery phase: a small set of source IPs hitting many of the org's FortiGate edge IPs on TCP/443, TCP/541 or TCP/10443 against the FortiGate-specific URI surface (/remote/login, /remote/logincheck, /sslvpn/portal, /api/v2/cmdb, /api/v2/monitor) at a rate no human reconnaissance would produce. Rationale: Article reports the agent queued 2,516 FortiGate devices across 106 countries; the queueing step is observable as inbound scanning of FortiGate management/SSL-VPN endpoints. The dcount(target)>=20 threshold separates a single misconfigured scanner from a fleet sweep. Cross-checked against Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR advisories and the Cybersecurity Advisory AA24-038A which document the same URI patterns adversaries target. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortiguard.com/psirt • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595/002/
ATT&CKT1595.001 T1595.002 T1590
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7) configured to probe internet-edge appliances
  • Authorized red-team / pentest engagements using nmap / wfuzz against FortiGate management surface
  • BAS platform (Picus, AttackIQ, SafeBreach) recon modules running on an approved test window
  • Shodan/Censys-style research scanners hitting the public IP that happens to host FortiGate
  • Misconfigured load-balancer health probes hammering /remote/login endpoint
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<authorized-scanner-asn-ips>"])) and SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<bas-platform-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull WHOIS/ASN for SourceIP and check against the authorized-scanner allowlist and the published Cybersecurity-Advisory IOC feed; review whether DistinctTargets covers your full FortiGate fleet or a subset. 2) Contain: if SourceIP is unknown infrastructure, block at the edge ACL and quarantine the targeted FortiGates pending creds-rotation; if any of those FortiGates later show a successful login from the same SourceIP within 24h, declare incident. 3) Hunt: pivot on SourceIP across DeviceNetworkEvents / CommonSecurityLog for the past 30d to find earlier reconnaissance, and confirm none of your FortiGate admin accounts use weak/default passwords by reviewing FortiManager password-policy compliance.
let WindowSize = 5m;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct has "FortiGate"
| where (Activity has_any ("login","auth-logon-fail","ssl-vpn-login","admin-login"))
     or (RequestURL has_any ("/remote/login","/remote/logincheck","/sslvpn/","/api/v2/cmdb","/api/v2/monitor"))
| summarize 
    RequestCount = count(),
    DistinctTargets = dcount(DeviceExternalID),
    DistinctURIs = dcount(RequestURL),
    SampleURIs = make_set(RequestURL, 10),
    SampleTargets = make_set(DeviceExternalID, 10)
    by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowSize)
| where DistinctTargets >= 20 and RequestCount >= 100
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:syslog (@DeviceVendor:Fortinet OR @log_source:fortigate) (@RequestURL:(*remote/login* OR *remote/logincheck* OR *sslvpn/portal* OR *api/v2/cmdb* OR *api/v2/monitor*) OR @Activity:(login OR auth-logon-fail OR ssl-vpn-login OR admin-login))

FortiGate admin / SSL-VPN credential spray (one source, many users, few attempts each) AIExploitation High
Detects the credential-access phase of the February 2026 MCP-orchestrated FortiGate campaign: industrialized brute-force / password-spray against weak admin and SSL-VPN credentials, where one source IP touches many distinct usernames or many distinct FortiGate devices in a short window — the opposite shape from a forgetful user. Rationale: Article: 'no zero-days needed, just weak credentials, industrialized through a custom MCP server running offensive tools autonomously' — the actor's own logs queued 2,516 devices, so spray-shape (one source → many users/devices, low-count-per-user) is the diagnostic pattern. Thresholds calibrated to AWS's confirmed 600+ compromised devices across 55+ countries (i.e. the spray hit the full IPv4 internet, not 2-3 known FortiGate admin endpoints). Cross-checked vs MITRE T1110 sub-techniques and the Anthropic/AWS Feb-2026 disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/003/ • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1110.003 T1110.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Single source IP doing helpdesk-driven password reset cycles for many users
  • Misconfigured automation account looping a stale credential against many FortiGates
  • Authorized credential audit / BAS run sweeping known-weak passwords on a test schedule
  • Mobile SSL-VPN clients on a single NAT-ed corporate IP hitting many devices after a VPN cert rotation
  • Pen-testers running CrackMapExec / Hydra against FortiGate per scope-of-work
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<helpdesk-natpool>","<vpn-concentrator-ips>","<bas-platform-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: cross-reference SourceIP against your VPN-concentrator NAT pool, helpdesk source-IP allowlist, and any approved pentest/BAS engagement schedule; pull the list of UsersSeen and check if any are valid admin accounts. 2) Contain: if SourceIP is external infrastructure, block at the edge and force-rotate any credential the spray named (cleartext usernames in spray attempts reveal what the actor THINKS your admin accounts are called); enable lockout-after-N on FortiGate admin and SSL-VPN profiles if not already configured. 3) Hunt: query for any login *success* from the same SourceIP across the next 24h on any FortiGate (UC3 logic); if a success exists, treat as confirmed initial-access and escalate.
let WindowSize = 10m;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct has "FortiGate"
| where (Activity has_any ("login fail","auth-logon-fail","ssl-vpn login fail","admin login fail","authentication failed"))
     or DeviceEventClassID in ("32002","32021","32007","32004")
| summarize 
    FailCount = count(),
    DistinctUsers = dcount(SourceUserName),
    DistinctTargets = dcount(DeviceExternalID),
    UsersSeen = make_set(SourceUserName, 30),
    TargetsSeen = make_set(DeviceExternalID, 20),
    FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastFail = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowSize)
| where (DistinctUsers >= 10 and FailCount >= 20) or (DistinctTargets >= 5 and FailCount >= 15)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:syslog (@DeviceVendor:Fortinet OR @log_source:fortigate) (@Activity:(*login*fail* OR *auth-logon-fail* OR *ssl-vpn*fail* OR *admin*login*fail*) OR @DeviceEventClassID:(32002 OR 32021 OR 32007 OR 32004))

First-ever successful FortiGate admin/SSL-VPN auth from new ASN immediately after burst of failures AIInstallation High
Detects the moment the spray works: a successful FortiGate admin or SSL-VPN authentication from a SourceIP that the org has never authenticated from before, within 10 minutes of a credential-failure burst from that same SourceIP. This is the article's initial-access step — 'AWS confirmed 600+ devices across 55+ countries' — and the highest-fidelity single signal in this campaign. Rationale: Article: the actor's MCP-driven workflow sprayed then succeeded — AWS confirmed 600+ devices compromised. The 'never seen this SourceIP succeed before + burst of failures within last 10m' shape is exactly the spray-to-foothold transition and is extremely hard for a normal user to trigger. Cross-checked against MITRE T1133 and the Fortinet-PSIRT pattern of weak-credential abuse. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1133/ • https://www.fortiguard.com/psirt

  • M&A integration where a new partner's NAT range starts authenticating into FortiGate SSL-VPN
  • Mobile SSL-VPN client whose carrier rotated the egress IP mid-session
  • Authorized red-team that completed a spray engagement with one valid credential

| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<corp-nat-ranges>","<approved-mssp-ips>","<bas-platform-ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull WHOIS/ASN/geo for SourceIP; if it's hosting infrastructure (DigitalOcean, OVH, Hetzner, AWS) and not a residential ISP, treat as hostile until proven otherwise. Identify SourceUserName and whether it's a privileged admin or a regular VPN user. 2) Contain: disable the compromised account, force MFA-everywhere on FortiGate (admin AND SSL-VPN profile), rotate the secret, terminate the active SSL-VPN session via FortiGate CLI, and block SourceIP at the edge. 3) Hunt: from the moment of successful auth, pivot to UC4 (sub-second CLI-cadence) and UC5 (LLM-API egress from the FortiGate) on the same DeviceExternalID; pull config changes and admin actions on that FortiGate for the next 24h.

Sub-second FortiGate CLI / API burst from a single admin session (MCP machine-cadence) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the article's execution phase: after foothold, the MCP server drives the appliance autonomously, calling config/diagnose/exec/cmdb endpoints sub-second apart in one session — a cadence no human admin produces (Wireshark-fast typing tops out around 1-2 cmd/sec, not 5-10/sec sustained for dozens of commands). Rationale: Article: 'a custom MCP server running offensive tools autonomously' — autonomous LLM agents call tools sub-second; humans don't. The rate-per-second threshold (>=5/s sustained over >=20 commands) catches the MCP cadence without flagging FortiManager push-config jobs, which use bulk/transactional commits not per-command CLI lines. Cross-checked vs how MCP servers serialise tool calls (JSON-RPC requests batched at LLM-thinking rate, not human-typing rate). Cross-checked against: • https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1119/
ATT&CKT1059 T1106 T1119
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Network_Sessions.All_Sessions
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • FortiManager push-config job committing a large policy batch to a managed FortiGate
  • Ansible / Terraform automation deploying or auditing config in CI
  • FortiGate backup-config script pulling config sections sequentially
  • BAS platform running an authorized post-exploit scenario on a test FortiGate
  • Engineer using fortios-cli automation library to bulk-tune QoS rules
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<fortimanager-ip>","<ansible-controller>","<terraform-runner>","<bas-platform-ips>"])) and SourceUserName !in (dynamic(["svc-fortimanager","svc-ansible","svc-backup"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SourceIP/SourceUserName isn't FortiManager, your CI/CD jump host, or an approved automation account; inspect SampleCmds — read-heavy enumeration ('show', 'get sys interface', 'diagnose firewall', 'config router static' read), is the signature of recon-and-pivot rather than legitimate ops. 2) Contain: kill the active admin session via `execute logout admin`, disable the account, and snapshot the running-config + recent log buffer before the actor wipes it. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 (was this session preceded by a brand-new-ASN success?) and UC5 (did this FortiGate then originate LLM-API egress?); also query Change datamodel for any added admin accounts, new VPN users, or modified route/policy rules in the same session window.
let WindowSize = 10s;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct has "FortiGate"
| where Activity has_any ("config","exec","diagnose","cmdb","get sys","show ","api-call")
     or DeviceEventClassID has_any ("00043","00044","41001","43008")
| summarize 
    CmdCount = count(),
    FirstCmd = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastCmd = max(TimeGenerated),
    SampleCmds = make_set(DeviceCustomString1, 20),
    SampleActivities = make_set(Activity, 10)
    by SourceUserName, SourceIP, DeviceExternalID, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowSize)
| extend DurationSec = todouble(datetime_diff('millisecond', LastCmd, FirstCmd)) / 1000.0
| extend RatePerSec = todouble(CmdCount) / (DurationSec + 0.1)
| where CmdCount >= 20 and RatePerSec >= 5
| order by RatePerSec desc
source:syslog (@DeviceVendor:Fortinet OR @log_source:fortigate) (@Activity:(*config* OR *exec* OR *diagnose* OR *cmdb* OR *api-call*) OR @DeviceEventClassID:(00043 OR 00044 OR 41001 OR 43008))
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count as cmd_count, min(_time) as first_cmd, max(_time) as last_cmd, values(All_Changes.command) as commands, values(All_Changes.object) as objects from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.dest_app="fortigate" OR All_Changes.dest_app="fortios" by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.dest, All_Changes.session_id, _time span=10s | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | eval duration_sec = last_cmd - first_cmd | eval rate_per_sec = cmd_count / (duration_sec + 0.1) | where cmd_count >= 20 AND rate_per_sec >= 5 | sort 0 - rate_per_sec
| tstats summariesonly=false count as cmd_count, min(_time) as first_cmd, max(_time) as last_cmd, values(All_Changes.command) as commands, values(All_Changes.object) as objects from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.dest_app="fortigate" OR All_Changes.dest_app="fortios" by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.dest, All_Changes.session_id, _time span=10s | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | eval duration_sec = last_cmd - first_cmd | eval rate_per_sec = cmd_count / (duration_sec + 0.1) | where cmd_count >= 20 AND rate_per_sec >= 5 | sort 0 - rate_per_sec
Outbound LLM API / MCP JSON-RPC egress from network appliance or jump host AICommand & Control High
Detects the article's command-and-control shape: a custom MCP server brokers tasks between the LLM and compromised fleet over web protocols. Inverts the assumption — network appliances (FortiGate, PA, Cisco) and edge jump hosts have no business calling api.anthropic.com / api.openai.com / Bedrock-runtime endpoints. First-seen outbound JSON-RPC or LLM-completion traffic from those device classes is a high-fidelity C2 indicator. Rationale: Article: 'a custom MCP server running offensive tools autonomously' brokering between LLM and compromised fleet over web protocols. FortiGate appliances do not legitimately call Anthropic/OpenAI/Bedrock; engineering laptops do. Restricting scope via DeviceInfo.DeviceCategory == 'NetworkDevice' or MachineGroup tags eliminates the developer-workstation FP class. Cross-checked vs MCP spec (JSON-RPC over HTTPS) and the Anthropic May-2026 disclosure of Claude Mythos use. Cross-checked against: • https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification • https://www.anthropic.com/news • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/002/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002 T1568
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned in-appliance AI assistant feature reaching out to vendor's AI back-end (FortiGate FortiAI, PA Prisma AI)
  • Engineering laptop tagged as 'jumpbox' in MachineGroup due to inventory mis-classification
  • Cloud-native bastion (AWS SSM session-manager host) running an authorized Bedrock-powered chat tool
  • FortiAnalyzer's outbound license-check that happens to TLS-handshake to a CloudFront edge sharing IP with LLM CDN
  • Authorized red-team / BAS test that purposely simulates LLM-driven C2 to validate this very detection
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Code.exe","cursor.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")) and not (MachineGroup has_any ("dev-workstations","engineering-laptops")) and DeviceName !startswith "DEV-" and DeviceName !startswith "ENG-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm DeviceName really is an appliance/edge host (not a misclassified workstation); inspect InitiatingProcessFileName — if it's a stock OS process (httpd, openssl, curl invoked from the appliance shell) on an appliance that has no vendor-AI feature, treat as confirmed C2. 2) Contain: drop egress from that DeviceExternalID to all LLM-API FQDNs at the proxy, snapshot the appliance config + memory if supported, and isolate the appliance from the management plane; if a FortiGate, immediately rotate all admin and SSL-VPN credentials and revoke all active sessions. 3) Hunt: pivot on RemoteIP across DeviceNetworkEvents for any other internal host calling the same LLM endpoint with similar User-Agent / cadence; also pull UC3 successful-auth events for the same appliance over the prior 7d and any UC4 sub-second CLI bursts on the same DeviceExternalID.
let LlmApiHosts = dynamic(["api.anthropic.com","api.openai.com","bedrock-runtime","generativelanguage.googleapis.com","claude.ai"]);
let LlmApiPaths = dynamic(["/v1/messages","/v1/chat/completions","/v1/complete","/jsonrpc"]);
let ApplianceDevices = DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, DeviceCategory, DeviceType, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup) by DeviceId, DeviceName
    | where DeviceCategory == "NetworkDevice"
        or DeviceType == "NetworkDevice"
        or IsInternetFacing == true
        or MachineGroup has_any ("firewall","appliance","jumpbox","jumphost","bastion","edge");
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (LlmApiHosts) or RemoteUrl has_any (LlmApiPaths)
| join kind=inner ApplianceDevices on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceCategory, DeviceType, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LlmApiDomains = dynamic(["api.anthropic.com","api.openai.com","bedrock-runtime","generativelanguage.googleapis.com","claude.ai"]);
let LlmApiPaths = dynamic(["/v1/messages","/v1/chat/completions","/v1/complete","/jsonrpc"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor in~ ("Fortinet","Palo Alto Networks","Cisco","Check Point","Juniper","SonicWall")
| where DestinationDnsDomain has_any (LlmApiDomains)
     or RequestURL has_any (LlmApiDomains)
     or RequestURL has_any (LlmApiPaths)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceExternalID, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: LLM API or MCP JSON-RPC Egress From Network Appliance or Edge Host
id: 1f8c4b3e-7a52-4d61-9c4e-2b9d6a14e1f0
description: Detects outbound connections from network appliances, firewalls, or edge jump hosts to LLM API endpoints (Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock, Gemini) or generic JSON-RPC paths — the C2 channel of the MCP-orchestrated FortiGate campaign described in TheHackerNews 2026-06-11 article.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ai-broke-vulnerability-management-thats.html
  - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification
author: detection-engineering
date: 2026/06/11
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1102.002
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_domain:
    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - 'api.anthropic.com'
      - 'api.openai.com'
      - 'bedrock-runtime'
      - 'generativelanguage.googleapis.com'
      - 'claude.ai'
  filter_dev_workstations:
    Image|contains:
      - '\Code.exe'
      - '\cursor.exe'
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
  condition: selection_domain and not filter_dev_workstations
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationHostname:(api.anthropic.com OR api.openai.com OR claude.ai OR generativelanguage.googleapis.com) OR @DestinationHostname:*bedrock-runtime*)) OR (source:syslog (@DeviceVendor:Fortinet OR @log_source:fortigate OR @log_source:paloalto OR @log_source:cisco-asa) (@DestinationDnsDomain:(api.anthropic.com OR api.openai.com OR claude.ai OR generativelanguage.googleapis.com) OR @DestinationDnsDomain:*bedrock-runtime* OR @RequestURL:(*v1/messages* OR *v1/chat/completions* OR *jsonrpc*)))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/(api\.anthropic\.com|api\.openai\.com|bedrock-runtime|generativelanguage\.googleapis\.com|claude\.ai)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())
| count > 1
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.type, requestParameters.modelId, awsRegion
| filter eventSource = "bedrock-runtime.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["InvokeModel","InvokeModelWithResponseStream","Converse","ConverseStream"]
      and userIdentity.type in ["IAMUser","AssumedRole","Root"]
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
| stats count(*) as invocations, count_distinct(sourceIPAddress) as src_ips, earliest(@timestamp) as first_seen, latest(@timestamp) as last_seen by userIdentity.arn, requestParameters.modelId, sourceIPAddress
| filter invocations > 50
| sort invocations desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count, values(Web.url) as urls, sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out, sum(Web.bytes_in) as bytes_in, dc(Web.dest) as dest_count from datamodel=Web where (Web.dest IN ("api.anthropic.com","api.openai.com","claude.ai","generativelanguage.googleapis.com") OR Web.dest="*bedrock-runtime*" OR Web.url IN ("*/v1/messages*","*/v1/chat/completions*","*/v1/complete*","*/jsonrpc*")) AND (Web.src_category IN ("network_appliance","firewall","dmz_jumphost","bastion") OR Web.src IN ("<edge_appliance_subnets>")) by Web.src_ip, Web.dest, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort 0 - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Web.url) as urls, sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out, sum(Web.bytes_in) as bytes_in, dc(Web.dest) as dest_count from datamodel=Web where (Web.dest IN ("api.anthropic.com","api.openai.com","claude.ai","generativelanguage.googleapis.com") OR Web.dest="*bedrock-runtime*" OR Web.url IN ("*/v1/messages*","*/v1/chat/completions*","*/v1/complete*","*/jsonrpc*")) AND (Web.src_category IN ("network_appliance","firewall","dmz_jumphost","bastion") OR Web.src IN ("<edge_appliance_subnets>")) by Web.src_ip, Web.dest, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort 0 - count
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("zerodayclock.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["zerodayclock.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("zerodayclock.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("zerodayclock.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("zerodayclock.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("zerodayclock.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

OceanLotus Hits Vietnam Investors With SPECTRALVIPER in FireAnt Attack

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 16 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The Vietnam-aligned threat actor known as OceanLotus has been attributed to two distinct campaigns that targeted domestic entities and stock investors with a backdoor known as SPECTRALVIPER. The campaigns involve a prolonged cyber espionage operation aimed at a Vietnamese infrastructure and transport construction corporation between mid-2024 and February 2026, as well as a supply chain attack

FireAnt Metakit.exe pulling tampered setup.exe from update server AIDelivery High
Hunts the supply-chain entry point: legitimate Metakit.exe fetching an unsigned setup.exe from the metakit.fireant.vn/Software/ update path. ESET noted version.xml lacks signature validation, so any setup.exe pull during the Oct 2025–Mar 2026 window is suspect. Rationale: Article names Metakit.exe and the exact URL path metakit.fireant.vn/Software/version.xml + setup.exe as the supply-chain delivery vector; absence of signature validation means any pull during/after the campaign window is suspect. Cross-checked ESET write-up via the article body; no second-source IOC validation needed since this is a campaign-specific URL. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105
Data sourcesWeb.Web Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Metakit auto-update during pre-Oct-2025 / post-Mar-2026 windows (drop from time-bound)
  • Investor support engineer manually downloading version.xml via browser, not via Metakit.exe
  • Internal IT mirror/test environment pointing Metakit at metakit.fireant.vn
  • Endpoint hosting both Metakit.exe and a legitimately signed setup.exe
  • Sandbox detonation of Metakit.exe in security tool
Suppression filter
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2025-10-01) .. datetime(2026-04-01))
Response runbook
1) Triage: SHA1 the setup.exe written to disk; compare against the article's hash list (865A1739..., B0FEA981..., 48FEBB91..., 511B7745..., 8CD78B8D...). Check the device's user — is it a stock-investor profile? 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response, block metakit.fireant.vn at the proxy/EDR, kill Metakit.exe and any child of the dropped setup.exe. 3) Hunt: across the org, pivot on DNS for metakit.fireant.vn, on SHA1 of the dropped binary, and on subsequent loads of DtlCrashCatch.dll. Pull all hosts that ran Metakit.exe in the campaign window for forensic imaging.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "Metakit.exe"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("metakit.fireant.vn/Software/setup.exe","metakit.fireant.vn/Software/version.xml")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "setup.exe"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "Metakit.exe"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1
) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "metakit.fireant.vn/Software/" and (Url has "setup.exe" or Url has "version.xml")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FireAnt Metakit Pulls Tampered Update Binary

description: Detects the legitimate FireAnt Metakit.exe fetching an unsigned setup.exe / version.xml from metakit.fireant.vn — the entry point of the OceanLotus 2025-26 supply-chain compromise (ESET, June 2026).

DtlCrashCatch.dll side-loaded by signed binary (SPECTRALVIPER loader) AIInstallation High
Hunts the SPECTRALVIPER side-loading payload: a rogue DLL named DtlCrashCatch.dll loaded by any legitimate signed host process. ESET identified this as the loader DLL used across both the FireAnt and the Transport Construction Corp intrusions. Rationale: DtlCrashCatch.dll is the specific rogue DLL named in the article as the SPECTRALVIPER side-load payload. The name has no legitimate Windows / vendor counterpart, so a single hit is high-confidence.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic analyst loading the sample in a sandboxed analysis tool
  • EDR/AV vendor pushing the DLL to a quarantine path as an IOC
  • Threat-intel platform unpacking the sample for static analysis
  • Honeypot or red-team kit purposely staging the file
  • Backup software accessing the DLL during full-disk scan
Suppression filter
| where LoaderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\" and LoaderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\Defender\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the signed loader binary, capture its SHA256, confirm the parent process tree, and pull the DLL for hash comparison to the article's SHA1 list. 2) Contain: isolate the device, kill the loader process, block the DLL hash via Defender custom indicator, quarantine the file. 3) Hunt: search org-wide for any host that has ever loaded DtlCrashCatch.dll, then pivot to network telemetry for financemachinelearning[.]com / gatewayrvcenter[.]com from those hosts within ±24h.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where FileName =~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256,
          LoaderImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          LoaderPath  = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          LoaderCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where LoaderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\" and LoaderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\"
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe injection target for SPECTRALVIPER AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the SPECTRALVIPER hollowing/injection step: legitimate OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe receiving remote thread / image injection then beaconing to the article's C2 domains. ESET specifies OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe as the injection victim. Rationale: OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe never legitimately calls the six OceanLotus C2 domains or the eight associated IPs. ESET identifies it as the specific injection target for SPECTRALVIPER, so process+destination correlation is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1055.012 T1055.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel detonation of SPECTRALVIPER in a Defender Live Response sandbox on the SOC's own jump host
  • Red-team simulation of the OceanLotus chain on a sanctioned host
  • Researcher mirror of the C2 infrastructure for tracking
  • Mistyped allow-list entry that resolves a similar-looking domain to one of these IPs
  • Personal OneDrive client on a BYOD device through a proxy that NATs to a flagged IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe parent process — legitimate launches come from explorer.exe / OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe; an unusual parent (e.g. msdtc.exe, a signed loader, or services.exe via svchost.exe) confirms injection. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block all six C2 domains + eight IPs at the proxy and EDR, preserve memory image for SPECTRALVIPER reversing. 3) Hunt: search 90 days back for DtlCrashCatch.dll loads on the same host, for prior Metakit.exe → setup.exe writes, and for any beacons from the listed IP set across the org. Pivot to MSSQL telemetry on the same subnet for the transport-construction TTP (sqlservr.exe → cmd / powershell).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com")
   or RemoteIP in ("38.60.245.37","139.99.33.239","139.162.11.152","139.180.128.42","142.91.98.77","166.88.77.186","194.68.26.241","103.119.47.104")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where DstHostname has_any ("financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com")
   or DstIpAddr in ("38.60.245.37","139.99.33.239","139.162.11.152","139.180.128.42","142.91.98.77","166.88.77.186","194.68.26.241","103.119.47.104")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol

sqlservr.exe spawning shells (OceanLotus MSSQL initial access) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the suspected initial-access path used in the Vietnamese transport-construction intrusion: exploitation of a public-facing Microsoft SQL Server leading to xp_cmdshell-style child processes off sqlservr.exe. ESET says the access was retained Nov 2024 → Feb 2026. Rationale: Article calls out exploitation of a public-facing MSSQL server as the suspected initial-access vector for the transport-construction campaign; sqlservr.exe → shell/LOLBin is the canonical post-exploit signature (xp_cmdshell, sp_OACreate, or CLR abuse).
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1505.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate DBA running xp_cmdshell-driven maintenance scripts during change windows
  • SCCM / SQL Server installer launching child processes during patching
  • Sentry / Datadog SQL Server integration scripts calling powershell.exe
  • Backup product (e.g. SQLBackupAndFTP) shelling out to BAT scripts
  • Vendor support session via the SQL Server Agent
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has "WSUS" and ChildCmd !has "DISM" and ParentImage !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\MSSQL\\Binn\Cluster"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm sqlservr.exe service account, whether xp_cmdshell is enabled on the instance, and review SQL audit log for sp_configure or unusual logins from external IPs ahead of the spawn. 2) Contain: disable xp_cmdshell, rotate the sa credential, reset all SQL logins, block external 1433/UDP1434 at the perimeter if the server is not meant to be public. 3) Hunt: pivot to ImageLoads for DtlCrashCatch.dll and to outbound traffic from this device for gatewayrvcenter[.]com; sweep the subnet for additional SPECTRALVIPER variants (article notes three different variants observed in this network).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sqlservr.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "sqlservr.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SPECTRALVIPER known-bad file hash on host AIInstallation Medium
Hash-based alert for the five SHA1s ESET published as SPECTRALVIPER components (downloaders / loader / backdoor variants observed across the FireAnt and transport-construction intrusions). Rationale: Five SHA1s pulled directly from the article's IOC list. A hash hit on process create, file write, or image load is article-specific and high-confidence; no second-source corroboration needed because the hash itself is the IOC.
ATT&CKT1027 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst running the IOC sample inside a sanctioned malware analysis VM
  • EDR signature ingest writing the sample to a quarantine folder for vendor analysis
  • Threat-intel team detonating the sample in a Cuckoo / Joe Sandbox
  • Forensic acquisition of a previously infected host bringing the artifact onto SOC infrastructure
  • Backup or DLP product accessing the file during retention scan
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA1 hit, capture file path + parent process, identify the user — investor / DBA / generic workstation? 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the SHA1 hashes via Defender custom indicators and the perimeter sandbox, preserve memory + disk. 3) Hunt: pivot to network telemetry for the six C2 domains and eight IPs from the same host ±30 days; check whether Metakit.exe was ever installed (FireAnt vector) or whether sqlservr.exe spawned children (transport vector).
let badSha1 = dynamic(["865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D","B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194","48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947","511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB","8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA1 in (badSha1) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine, Surface="Process"),
  (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA1 in (badSha1) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Surface="FileWrite"),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA1 in (badSha1) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Surface="ImageLoad")
| order by Timestamp desc
let badSha1 = dynamic(["865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D","B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194","48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947","511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB","8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037"]);
union
  (ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d) | where SHA1 in (badSha1) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1, Surface="Process"),
  (ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d) | where TargetFileSHA1 in (badSha1) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, SHA1=TargetFileSHA1, ActingProcessCommandLine, Surface="FileWrite")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Run-key persistence pointing at SPECTRALVIPER staging paths AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the persistence step OceanLotus typically uses: HKLM/HKCU Run / RunOnce writes whose data points at AppData / ProgramData / Temp executables or DLLs side-loaded by signed binaries — the shape SPECTRALVIPER needs to survive reboot. Rationale: OceanLotus chain ends with SPECTRALVIPER injected into OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe — that needs disk persistence to survive reboot, and the loader DLL (DtlCrashCatch.dll) must be pointed at via Run/RunOnce or a service. AppData/ProgramData/Temp paths in Run keys are the classic shape; combining with the campaign-specific DLL name keeps fidelity high.
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate per-user installer (e.g. Zoom, Slack updater) writing AppData paths into Run keys
  • Browser auto-update tasks (Chrome, Edge) refreshing Run entries
  • Steam / gaming launchers persisting in HKCU Run
  • Adobe Creative Cloud / OneDrive Standalone Updater refreshing their auto-start
  • Vendor LOB software installed for individual investors that lives in %LocalAppData%
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDriveSetup.exe","OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","chrome_installer.exe","MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe","AdobeARM.exe","AcroCEF.exe","Slack.exe","Teams.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the registry value, follow the path on disk, hash the target binary/DLL, check signing — unsigned + path matches the SPECTRALVIPER staging shape = high confidence. 2) Contain: delete the Run/RunOnce value, isolate the host, quarantine the referenced file, capture process memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing-process identity (InitiatingProcessFileName) for additional persistence (Services, Scheduled Tasks, WMI), and on the same DLL filename across the org via DeviceImageLoadEvents.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce")
| where RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", "DtlCrashCatch")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","OneDriveSetup.exe","TeamsSetup.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce")
| where RegistryValueData has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", "DtlCrashCatch")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or SHA1 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or MD5 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or SHA1 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or MD5 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PeopleSoft Internet Architecture gadget-chain deserialization exploitation · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
